notes: Planning enforcement immunity under section 25 GLC Act 1973; Inspector decision upheld on section 171B ten-year immunity.

enrichment.short_title: Temporary sleeping accommodation: ten-year immunity and section 25 deeming
key_facts: Fairstate Ltd appealed an Inspector's decision upholding an enforcement notice alleging unlawful change of use of Flat 3 at Marylebone High Street from permanent residential to temporary sleeping accommodation.
The appeal was confined to ground (d): whether enforcement action was time-barred under the ten-year immunity in section 171B of the 1990 Act.
Occupation records showed largely short-term lettings under 90 days, but Miss Kapoor's continuous occupation for about 155 days in 1999 broke the immunity period.
The Inspector found lawful temporary sleeping use until early 1999, but resumption after Kapoor's occupation amounted to a fresh material change of use.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 289(6) of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 against an Inspector's decision on an enforcement notice appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Inspector's decision upheld; Westminster City Council denied separate costs but the Secretary of State awarded £5,000 costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where section 25 of the 1973 GLC Act applies, a change back from other residential use to temporary sleeping accommodation is deemed a material change of use even if immunity had previously accrued under section 171B; lawful immune use may end on such a change without abandonment or a new planning unit.
legal_issues: Whether ten-year immunity under section 171B survived Kapoor's occupation
Effect of section 25 deeming provisions on resumed temporary sleeping accommodation use
Whether immune lawful use is equivalent to planning permission for all purposes
Scope of section 57(4) where the last lawful use before the complained-of use differed

notes: Landmark combined appeals on high-earner periodical payments; section 25A clean-break duty and percentage-share term orders.

enrichment.short_title: McFarlane and Parlour: income sharing and section 25A in big-money divorces
key_facts: Two conjoined appeals concerned wives seeking substantial periodical payments from high-earning husbands after capital had already been divided without a clean break.
Bennett J had reduced Mrs McFarlane's award from £250,000 to £180,000 per annum and awarded Mrs Parlour £212,500 per annum on joint-lives bases.
Both cases involved surplus income far exceeding the parties' needs, with three children in each family.
Practitioners had debated whether White v White equality principles should apply to income as well as capital.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Conjoined appeals with permission granted under stricter Access to Justice Act 1999 standards; Parlour cross-appeal permission dismissed.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; McFarlane: district judge's £250,000 order restored for a five-year term without index linking; Parlour: term order of about one-third of net income for four years substituted; husband's cross-appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: White v White fairness applies to periodical payments as well as capital; courts must apply section 25A and pursue a clean break where possible; in exceptional surplus-income cases term orders sharing a percentage of the earner's net income are preferable to indefinite joint-lives maintenance, with both parties sharing responsibility to invest surplus.
legal_issues: Whether equality yardstick from White applies to division of income
Application of section 25A duty to terminate financial obligations
Validity of indefinite joint-lives orders where capital clean break is impossible
Whether periodical payments may include an element of capitalisation or future provision

notes: Police constable's summary removal held unlawful; Regulation 14 retirement determination did not permit dismissal by conduct.

enrichment.short_title: Unlawful removal of police constable on sick leave
key_facts: PC Barwise went on long-term sick leave from April 2002 after alleging bullying at a public order training site.
After prolonged absence, non-attendance at occupational health appointments, and trips to Spain, the Chief Constable wrote in September 2003 terminating his office as constable.
Barwise challenged the decision as outside statutory powers, arguing retirement required one month's written notice under Regulation 14 and the Secretary of State's determination.
The force contended Barwise's conduct evidenced retirement or repudiatory acceptance at common law.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim challenging a Chief Constable's decision to remove a police constable from office.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; declaration that removal was unlawful; damages ordered for housing allowance; claimant awarded £7,000 costs; relief not refused on conduct grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 14 and Annex D permit retirement only on one month's written notice or shorter notice accepted by the authority; alleged misconduct or disengagement during sickness absence is not covered and must be addressed through conduct, efficiency, or medical retirement procedures, not summary removal.
legal_issues: Whether Regulation 14 permits treating conduct as short-notice retirement
Whether a constable's office may be terminated at common law by repudiatory breach
Whether judicial review relief should be refused for the claimant's conduct
Financial consequences of unlawful removal from office

notes: Leading Lord Chief Justice guidance on murder minimum terms under Criminal Justice Act 2003 Schedule 21 and transitional Schedule 22.

enrichment.short_title: Guidance on mandatory life minimum terms under the 2003 Act
key_facts: Four conjoined appeals tested minimum terms imposed after the 2003 Act transferred minimum-term decisions from the Secretary of State to trial judges following Anderson v Secretary of State.
Schedule 21 sets starting points of whole life, 30 years, 15 years, or 12 years depending on seriousness and age.
Schedule 22 paragraph 10 caps minimum terms for pre-commencement offences by reference to the Secretary of State's pre-December 2002 practice.
Individual appeals involved neighbour stabbing, bus-window bottle dispute murder, and Elener armed robbery murders.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Conjoined appeals against minimum terms set under section 269 after convictions for murder following the 2003 Act commencement.
enrichment.outcome: Guidance issued modifying use of May 2002 Practice Direction for post-May 2002 offences; Sullivan appeal dismissed; Gibbs minimum term reduced from 17 to 14 years; Elener appeals dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Judges retain discretion under section 269(3) while having regard to Schedule 21; for transitional cases paragraph 10 requires a two-stage assessment and, for offences after May 2002, the May 2002 Practice Direction best reflects the Secretary of State's prior practice; minimum terms address punishment and deterrence while public protection remains with the Parole Board.
legal_issues: How to apply Schedule 21 starting points and aggravating or mitigating factors
Interpretation of Schedule 22 paragraph 10 transitional cap
Which pre-2003 Practice Directions reflect Secretary of State practice
Whether Article 5 and Article 7 ECHR require use of May 2002 guidance

notes: Disability discrimination appeal; constructive dismissal held to be dismissal under DDA and half-pay reduction unlawful.

enrichment.short_title: Constructive dismissal and sick pay under the Disability Discrimination Act
key_facts: Mrs Meikle, a visually impaired teacher at Gedling School employed by Nottinghamshire County Council, resigned in May 2000 after years of failure to provide enlarged materials and adjusted timetables.
The tribunal upheld multiple DDA discrimination findings but rejected constructive dismissal, DDA dismissal, and half-pay discrimination claims.
The EAT reversed on all three rejected issues; the council appealed to the Court of Appeal.
Half-pay reduction after 100 days' sickness absence followed a council policy applied while reasonable adjustments remained unmade.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employer appeal to the Court of Appeal from an Employment Appeal Tribunal decision reversing an employment tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; EAT upheld on constructive dismissal, meaning of dismissal in section 4(2)(d), and unlawful half-pay reduction under sections 5 and 6.
enrichment.ratio: Constructive dismissal is a dismissal for DDA purposes; section 6(11) excludes pension and third-party insurance schemes but not contractual sick pay, so retaining full pay may be a reasonable adjustment; where section 6 is breached unjustifiably, section 5(5) prevents justification of less favourable treatment.
legal_issues: Whether resignation in response to failure to make reasonable adjustments was constructive dismissal
Whether constructive dismissal falls within dismissal in section 4(2)(d) DDA
Whether half-pay policy was excluded from section 6 duty by section 6(11)
Application of section 5(5) where reasonable adjustments were not made

notes: Interim receiver over charged properties upheld; Eliades' false deposition evidence supported nominee inference.

enrichment.short_title: Receiver appointment over judgment debtor's nominee charges
key_facts: Lennox Lewis obtained a US judgment against his former manager Panos Eliades and a reduced English judgment of about US$5.88 million.
Grigson J appointed a receiver over charges held by Managa Properties Ltd over two properties, restraining Managa from dealing with the charged debts.
The claimant contended Eliades was the beneficial owner of Managa and the charges, with assets held as nominee through Cypriot companies linked to his brother.
Eliades had given false deposition evidence in New York denying knowledge of Managa despite family connections.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to discharge an ex parte without-notice order appointing a receiver and granting injunctive relief against a third party.
enrichment.outcome: Application to discharge dismissed; receiver appointment and injunction continued subject to undertaking in damages; material non-disclosure on cross-undertaking and CPR 23.9 notification held insufficient to discharge.
enrichment.ratio: Where a judgment debtor has lied about connections to a charging company and a pattern of Cypriot nominee structures exists, there is a serious issue to be tried that assets are held for his benefit; balance of convenience favours maintaining the receiver where the claimant can satisfy an undertaking and refusal risks irrecoverable removal of assets.
legal_issues: Whether evidence supported appointment of a receiver over third-party charges
Whether ex parte non-disclosure justified discharge of the order
Balance of convenience on Mareva-type relief in aid of execution
Inference of beneficial ownership from false deposition evidence

notes: Loss-of-chance claim against negligent solicitors; 30% prospects assessment upheld despite causation findings.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitors' negligence: valuing lost professional negligence claim
key_facts: Clement Jones Solicitors allowed Mrs Dixon's negligence claim against accountants The Dyer Partnership to be struck out for failure to serve a statement of claim.
The underlying claim concerned negligent failure to warn about viability of a convenience store venture secured on Mrs Dixon's home after Barclays refused finance.
The trial judge found the accountants negligent but assessed lost claim value at 30% because Mrs Dixon would likely have proceeded despite warnings.
Mrs Dixon's credibility was criticised and her account of being persuaded to mortgage her home was rejected.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against assessment of damages for solicitors' negligence causing loss of underlying litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; 30% assessment of prospects of success in the lost claim upheld.
enrichment.ratio: In struck-out litigation cases the court assesses prospects of the underlying claim rather than conducting a trial within a trial; a finding that the claimant would probably have proceeded despite warnings goes to quantification of prospects, not to a balance-of-probabilities causation test requiring total failure of the solicitors' claim.
legal_issues: Whether loss of chance or balance-of-probabilities causation applies to struck-out claims
Whether 30% prospects assessment was perverse given likely continuation finding
Application of Kitchen v Royal Air Force Association and Mount v Barker Austin principles
Distinction from Allied Maples transaction-based causation analysis

notes: Trade mark opposition appeal dismissed; section 5(3) reputation link and detriment require evidence not inference.

enrichment.short_title: MASTERCARD opposition to CREDIT MASTER registration
key_facts: Mastercard opposed Hitachi Credit's application to register CREDIT MASTER for classes 9, 16, 35, 36 and 42.
Mastercard relied on reputation of MASTERCARD under section 5(3) after narrowing its case from 91 marks to five.
The hearing officer refused amendment to extend section 5(3) to similar goods following Davidoff and Adidas-Salomon ECJ decisions.
The officer found insufficient link between the marks and no evidence of unfair advantage or detriment despite MASTERCARD's fame.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on point of law from a Trade Marks Registry hearing officer decision to a Chancery Division judge under CPR 52.11.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; refusal of CREDIT MASTER registration not ordered; costs assessment remitted on technical grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Section 5(3) requires proof of a link between marks and actual unfair advantage or detriment, not mere theoretical dilution; reputation alone does not dispense with evidential requirements; similarity is assessed globally as in section 5(2) but without requiring likelihood of confusion.

Correct test for link under section 5(3) after Adidas-Salomon and Davidoff

notes: Costs ruling after Wasps' valuation negligence win; full costs, indemnity basis from Part 36 date, CFA relief granted.

enrichment.short_title: Wasps costs after successful negligence claim against valuers
key_facts: Wasps Football Club trustees succeeded in a professional negligence claim against Lambert Smith Hampton over undervaluation of the Sudbury ground, recovering about £2.42 million principal.
Litigation was funded by a CFA with a 100% success fee; Form N251 was not served though the CFA was disclosed in correspondence.
Wasps amended their claim from reliance on a £5.7m DTZ valuation to Mr Lomax's £3.42m expert valuation after mediation failed.
Wasps made a Part 36 offer of £2.163m; LSH made a lower without-prejudice offer but no Part 36 offer.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Costs and interim payment applications following principal judgment in a commercial negligence trial.
enrichment.outcome: Wasps entitled to full costs without deduction; enhanced interest at 6% on damages from Part 36 expiry; costs on indemnity basis from 13 January 2004 but no interest on costs; costs stay granted pending appeal with liberty to apply; CFA sanction relief granted.
enrichment.ratio: Commercial winners ordinarily recover costs under CPR 44.3; failure to serve Form N251 may be relieved where the opponent knew of the CFA and suffered no prejudice; CPR 36.21 additional interest and indemnity costs should follow where a Part 36 offer is beaten unless unjust.
legal_issues: Whether Wasps should recover full costs despite amended valuation case
Relief from sanction under rule 44.3B for failure to file Form N251

notes: CCRC reference; fresh Asperger's evidence led to murder quashed and manslaughter substituted with life sentence.

enrichment.short_title: Murder conviction quashed on fresh Asperger's diminished responsibility evidence
key_facts: Reynolds, aged 17, killed pharmacist Anita De Souza with a claw hammer in February 1987 to steal shop takings and flee to France.
At trial medical evidence on personality was excluded from the intent issue; he was convicted of murder and detained at Her Majesty's pleasure.
CCRC referral followed later reports diagnosing Asperger's Syndrome, a condition not widely recognised at trial.
Fresh psychiatric evidence indicated substantially diminished responsibility; adjournment for secure hospital assessment was refused.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by reference of the Criminal Cases Review Commission under section 69 of the Criminal Appeal Act 1995.
enrichment.outcome: Murder conviction quashed as unsafe; manslaughter on grounds of diminished responsibility substituted; life imprisonment imposed with six-year minimum term specified.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh credible psychiatric evidence that Asperger's Syndrome substantially impaired responsibility and would likely have led to manslaughter at trial renders a murder conviction unsafe under section 23; where the disorder is untreatable and the offender poses a serious risk, life imprisonment remains appropriate despite long time served.
legal_issues: Admissibility of fresh medical evidence on appeal
Whether Asperger's Syndrome amounts to abnormality of mind under section 2
Appropriate sentence after substitution of manslaughter verdict
Whether case should be adjourned for secure hospital treatability assessment
